questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the short "yes" answer in Chinese, and what is it really?
What is the short "no" answer, and what is it really?
To what single syllable may a "no" answer be reduced, and in which tone?
What does polite usage require after a reduced "no" answer?
Give a complete negative answer in Chinese to the question Tā shi Měiguo rén ma?
What is the short "yes" answer really, in terms of the longer answer?

answers.answer_text: It is really the verb "am" of the longer, more complete answer.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which tone does bù carry when a "no" answer is reduced to a single syllable?
Are the short answers shì and bú shi usually left on their own?

answers.answer_text: No — both are commonly followed by complete answers.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Yes, she is Chinese."
Write the Chinese for "No, she is not American."

answers.answer_text: Bú shi, tā bú shi Měiguo rén.

articles.text:
4. A: Nǐ shi Zhōngguo rén ma?               Are you Chinese?
   B: Bú shi.                               No.
   A: Nǐ shi Měiguo rén ma?                 Are you an American?
   B: Shì.                                  Yes, I am.

5. A: Mǎ Xiǎojiě shi Měiguo rén ma?         Is Miss Mǎ an American?
   B: Bú shi, tā bú shi Měiguo rén.         No, she is not American.
   A: Tā shi Zhōngguo rén ma?               Is she Chinese?
   B: Shì, tā shi Zhōngguo rén.             Yes, she is Chinese.

Notes on Nos. 4-5

The short "yes" answer shì is really the verb "am" of the longer, more complete answer. The short "no" answer bú shi is really the "am not" of the longer answer.

It is possible to reduce a "no" answer to bù (note the Falling tone), but polite usage requires that you follow it up with a more complete answer. Both the short answers shì and bú shi are commonly followed by complete answers.
